headline: KFF reports that US federal pilot programs are testing AI that acts more like a doctor, while the FDA has not yet set rules for judging its safety.
score_reason: Important direction of travel for Medicare patients, but a secondary summary of an earlier New York Times report; kept at the curator score.
importance_line: Medicare patients and doctors may soon deal with AI doing tasks once left to physicians, but the FDA says this new kind of tool is harder to judge and is still taking comment on how to do it.
source: KFF, citing The New York Times
summary: KFF's health-information newsletter The Monitor says, citing The New York Times, that more than 200 companies have won approval from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to test AI tools that can talk to patients, give therapy, diagnose and adjust treatment with less direct physician involvement, and that the FDA has allowed four of them for Medicare patients outside its standard approval process. The FDA says such systems may be harder to judge because their outputs can be unpredictable and change over time, it has set no rules for them yet, and it is taking public comment until 19 October 2026.
notes: KFF credits The New York Times for the pilot figures; the NYT article was not opened. Only the AI-in-care section of the newsletter is used.
